title: How I freed up 4GB of storage to avoid paying for Google One
summary: I cleared enough clutter to avoid paying for another monthly subscription.
body: Credit: Robert Triggs / Android Authority I’ve been cruising in Google’s free storage tier for as long as I can remember, backing up my Photos, emails, and even WhatsApp messages without ever spending a penny. But over the past few months, I’ve been creeping up to the 15GB cap (17GB in my case , as an old-timer who jumped through Google’s security hoops), leading to a barrage of Google One notifications urging me to upgrade to a paid storage tier. That’s never going to happen. The economics of starting out at just $1.99 a month for 100GB might not sound like much, but I know it won’t be many more years before I hit that limit, too. Then I’d be hooked: forking out $4.99 and then $9.99 every month, in perpetuity, for the luxury of having Google back up my odds and ends. Granted, Google One might be worth the cost if you want Gemini in your docs and double AI usage without forking out for yet another monthly plan. But for me, I’m happy just using the free allowance to keep the most recent things I need within quick reach. I could store everything else on a USB stick or external hard drive for cheap.

title: The Apple Watch Series 12 is still superb, but Google has caught up
summary: Has Apple done enough to make the Apple Watch Series 12 a great smartwatch that's worth buying?
body: What is it about the Apple Watch? I have worn and used dozens of smartwatches and fitness trackers over the last few years, and yet, if I want to use a smartwatch between reviewing them, it’s the Apple Watch I reach for. Over the last month I’ve worn the Apple Watch Series 12, the latest model in the range, to try and once-and-for-all understand its allure. I think I know, but I also know it doesn’t necessarily make the Series 12 a must-buy for everyone, and the question over whether it could prompt a switch to Apple’s ecosystem is an even harder one to answer this year.

body: Googlebooks promise a lot of things, including, but not limited to, premium hardware and Android integration. It’s the Apple-like ecosystem Google is finally giving its loyal users. We got a taste of this with Chromebooks, but ChromeOS never reached the pinnacle of laptop-Android convergence that Google initially teased. Googlebooks hope to rectify this . Googlebooks have had their fair share of ups and downs since their recent launch. While the hardware is definitely up to par, the software seems to be a little half-baked thus far. title: Boxshelf is a new Android front-end that turns your ROMs into a virtual collection
summary: This new front-end turns your ROMs into gorgeous virtual game boxes, just in case you miss your physical collection.
body: Credit: Hadlee Simons / Android Authority TL;DR A new Android front-end called Boxshelf has been released on GitHub. This launcher emphasizes box art, with games being displayed as 3D boxes that you can inspect. Boxshelf also includes a museum view to show off your games on a digital shelf. There’s no shortage of front-ends or launchers for Android handhelds . We’ve got staples like ES-DE and Beacon, while new entrants like Socket and Play Field Portal have also made their mark. However, Boxshelf is the latest front-end to land on Android, and it might be up your alley if you miss physical games. Boxshelf launched on GitHub yesterday as a gaming-focused front-end for Windows and Steam Deck, but the most recent update has brought an Android version. This version is designed for the dual-screen AYN Thor handheld (showing the game you’re on and its buttons), but it also works on other Android devices.

title: 4 reasons why I’d recommend a foldable (and 4 reasons why I wouldn’t)
summary: I love foldables, but the high price and hardware compromises make them difficult to recommend to everyone.
body: Foldable phones have come a long way. From the fragile, almost experimental devices of the early days, into reliable daily drivers that you can well and truly chuck around like any other phone. We are well past the days of peeling screen protectors and failing hinges, with modern devices offering proper IP resistance, good-enough cameras, and top-tier silicon. Despite the category’s relative maturity, I can’t really say that foldables are or should be the default choice for everyone. Like any other tech product, foldables too have pros and cons. title: Google Find Hub is catching up to Apple Find My with left-behind alerts
summary: Better late than never.
body: TL;DR Google has started rolling out “Notify when left behind” alerts for trackers in the Find Hub app on Android. The alerts currently work with item trackers but not with devices like headphones. By default, the feature skips notifications at the Home address saved in your Google Account. For the longest time, Google’s Find Hub suffered from a really obvious oversight that competitors like Apple’s Find My did not: missing support for Left-Behind reminders. This missing feature would have definitely held back the Pixel Tag when it went on sale on November 11. Fortunately, Google has some good news. Google has started rolling out support for “Notify when left behind” alerts for tags and trackers in the Find Hub app on Android, as first spotted by 9to5Google . We’ve previously spotted this feature in development , and it was also included in October’s Play Services update changelog. So its rollout isn’t surprising. However, it is a welcome addition to Find Hub’s capabilities.

The section includes dedicated layout controls allowing users to view pins in List, Grid, or Compact view independently of the main library view. This appears to be a server-side test rolling out to select Android and iOS users. Spotify is testing a revamped mobile layout for the Your Library tab that separates pinned items into a dedicated carousel shelf, according to user reports. The change comes against the backdrop of Spotify’s tightened Family plan location checks and reports of an AI-powered Remix add-on , and could give users some more reason to stick with the streaming service amidst these changes. As shared by Reddit user alright-alright–, the refreshed Your Library UI introduces a separate “Pins” section right below the top filter chips. Instead of forcing pinned playlists, albums, and podcasts to share the same feed layout as the rest of your collection, Spotify now gives them their own dedicated section.

You probably wouldn’t be surprised to know that a principle called Laver’s Law describes the cyclicity in fashion. Styles that were trendy two decades ago suddenly emerge again, while what was hip almost a decade ago becomes distasteful. And it goes on — or at least has for the last several decades in the postmodern era. Something similar is happening with accessories and gadgets, especially when it comes to music, as we witness a resurgence of retro tech and equipment. In recent months, several audio brands have hopped on the bandwagon, offering retro-looking products with modern features. Now, Sony is joining the club with a pair of wired headphones that look straight out of the 1980s — but with a modern spin. title: Google fixes daylight saving time bug affecting Nest and Lenovo smart home devices
summary: Nest and Lenovo devices are getting back on schedule.
body: TL;DR Google says it has resolved the daylight saving time issue that caused incorrect timers and alarms on some smart home devices. The confirmation comes through Google’s Nest Community account on Reddit, following reports involving Nest and Lenovo devices. Google is asking users still experiencing problems to report them. Smart homes in parts of Canada have spent the week struggling with something their owners rarely have to think about: telling the correct time. After several days of misplaced hours, unreliable alarms, and disrupted routines, Google says it has finally straightened things out. In replies to Reddit discussions, the official Google Nest Community account confirmed that the daylight saving time issue affecting timers and alarms has been resolved. The account also posted the same confirmation involving Lenovo Smart Clock devices, suggesting the fix extends beyond Google’s own hardware.

title: Taking a Gander at Utah’s Goosenecks
summary: The San Juan River has carved deep, improbably curvy meanders into the desert landscape.
body: Earth Observatory Science Earth Observatory Taking a Gander at Utah’s… Earth Earth Observatory Image of the Day EO Explorer Topics All Topics Atmosphere Land Heat & Radiation Life on Earth Human Dimensions Natural Events Oceans Remote Sensing Technology Snow & Ice Water More Content Collections Global Maps World of Change Articles Earth Matters Blog Blue Marble: Next Generation EO Kids Mission: Biomes About About Us Subscribe 🛜 RSS Contact Us Search October 6, 2026 Tens of millions of years ago, the San Juan River in what is now southern Utah shared some characteristics with today’s Mississippi River. In a bygone geologic era, the San Juan flowed across a relatively flat plain that formed in an ancient marine environment. Unencumbered by rugged terrain, the river was free to take a long, meandering path on its gradual journey downslope. But this part of the San Juan changed when geologic forces pushed the Colorado Plateau upward. title: Garmin isn’t ready to abandon power-efficient MIP displays on wearables, even as AMOLED improves
summary: AMOLED is catching up, but one important advantage is keeping MIP alive.
body: TL;DR Garmin COO Brad Trenkle says MIP displays aren’t disappearing anytime soon because they still offer advantages in battery life and outdoor visibility. Although Garmin’s AMOLED watches are becoming more power-efficient, they haven’t completely closed the endurance gap with MIP models. Garmin also sees potential for solar-powered OLED watches, although no such product has been announced. A quiet tug-of-war is happening on Garmin wrists. On one side, AMOLED displays are winning hearts with their rich colors, crisp graphics, and gorgeous watch faces. On the other, the less glamorous memory-in-pixel (MIP) screens are still winning endurance contests, especially when the sun is blazing and the nearest charger is miles away. Garmin is increasingly embracing the former, but it isn’t ready to retire the latter. Speaking to TechRadar , Garmin COO Brad Trenkle explained that battery life remains the biggest reason MIP displays still have a place in the company’s smartwatch lineup.

title: I love big Si-C batteries, but slow charging is a steep price to pay
summary: Bigger batteries sound great, but are slower charging speeds worth the extra capacity?
body: Credit: Robert Triggs / Android Authority If there’s been one major game changer for smartphone hardware in the past few years, it’s undoubtedly the adoption of silicon-carbon (Si-C) battery technology. By mixing traditional lithium-ion cells with silicon-carbon, manufacturers are able to greatly increase a battery’s storage capacity without a huge increase in its physical size, meaning better longevity for our smartphones. Even small amounts of added Si-C have been a game changer for battery capacities. After being stuck with 5,000mAh Li-ion cells as the upper limit for the best part of a decade, we’ve quickly seen capacities jump to 7,000mAh, 8,000mAh, and even 10,000mAh cells in the most advanced cases.

title: Nostalgia: This phone spoke to me like no other
summary: Camera in a smartphone body.
body: Credit: Robert Triggs / Android Authority I might be a bit jaded, but smartphones have become a bit boring. Don’t get me wrong, modern flagships are incredible pieces of technology. But across the board, what you get in terms of year-over-year upgrades are faster processors, better cameras, and slightly brighter screens, but there’s rarely a phone that makes me stop and go, “Wow.” Now that the market is more or less commoditized, I don’t think we’ll ever see that again. However, things were different a decade ago. Phone makers were experimenting with everything from modular designs to 3D displays. Some of those ideas were downright terrible, while others got folded into smartphones we have today. For me, no phone embodied that spirit quite like the Nokia Lumia 1020.

title: Android Auto’s endless calling loop is driving Pixel and Galaxy owners crazy
summary: Gemini knows the name to contact. Android Auto keeps asking.
body: TL;DR Some Pixel and Samsung Galaxy owners say Android Auto repeatedly asks who they want to call or message, even after they provide a contact’s name. Google’s Android Auto community specialists are collecting diagnostic details to investigate, but there’s no confirmed cause or fix yet. The complaints come as Gemini rolls out more widely in Android Auto. Making a hands-free call shouldn’t feel like an interrogation. You say a contact’s name, Android Auto places the call, and your hands stay on the wheel. But for some Pixel and Samsung Galaxy owners, that simple exchange has turned into an endless conversation with a particularly forgetful assistant. No matter how many times they repeat the name, Android Auto keeps asking the same question: Who do you want to call? The complaints have been piling up on Google’s support forums since early October, with reports involving the Pixel 10, Pixel 10 Pro, Galaxy S24, Galaxy S25 Ultra, and Galaxy S26. Both calling and texting are affected, leaving some drivers unable to reach their contacts through voice commands.

title: You can now play Switch 2 games on Android via emulators and native ports
summary: It's early days, but Switch 2 emulation and native ports show a lot of promise.
body: Credit: Oliver Cragg / Android Authority TL;DR We’ve seen the first Nintendo Switch 2 emulators on Android, although many games aren’t playable. We’ve also seen the BananaNative project, which enabled native ports of Donkey Kong Bananza and Mario Kart World on Android. It’s still early days for these projects, but it’s clear that Switch 2 emulation and native ports are progressing incredibly quickly. The Nintendo Switch 2 launched just over a year ago, but we weren’t expecting to see emulators or native ports on Android for a while yet. However, that’s exactly what’s happened in recent weeks. We’ve seen Nintendo Switch 2 emulators landing on various platforms in the last week or two, and they all seem to be ultimately based on the acclaimed Eden emulator for Nintendo Switch 1 titles. Android isn’t left out of the fun, as we’ve also seen Eden SX2A , which is based on the PokeDinner emulator for other platforms. In fact, PokeDinner is in turn based on the so-called Eglantine emulator. And that particular emulator is based on Eden-NS2, which is itself a fork of the original Eden emulator for Nintendo Switch 1 titles. Forking heck.
